classification.difficultyReason: Use a factorial ratio to establish and interpret equality conditions for consecutive coefficients.

children.label: a
children.prompt: By considering the ratio of the coefficients of $x^k$ and $x^{k+1}$, show that it is possible for two consecutive terms to have the same coefficient.

answer.short:
Yes. $\displaystyle\frac{\binom{n}{k}}{\binom{n}{k+1}}=\frac{k+1}{n-k}$, so equality occurs when $k=\frac{n-1}{2}$.

For odd $n$, the two middle coefficients are equal.
answer.worked:
The coefficients are $\binom{n}{k}$ and $\binom{n}{k+1}$. Their ratio is
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\binom{n}{k}}{\binom{n}{k+1}}&=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\frac{(k+1)!(n-k-1)!}{n!}\\\frac{\binom{n}{k}}{\binom{n}{k+1}}&=\frac{k+1}{n-k}.\end{align*}$$
For equal coefficients,
$$\begin{align*}\frac{k+1}{n-k}&=1\\k+1&=n-k\\k&=\frac{n-1}{2}.\end{align*}$$
For odd $n$, this is an integer and gives the two middle coefficients. Thus two consecutive coefficients can be equal.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Is it possible for three consecutive coefficients to be equal?

answer.short: No. There is at most one pair of consecutive equal coefficients.
answer.worked:
Three consecutive equal coefficients would require equality for the pairs starting at both $k$ and $k+1$. From part (a), this requires
$$k=\frac{n-1}{2}\qquad\text{and}\qquad k+1=\frac{n-1}{2},$$
which is impossible. Hence three consecutive coefficients cannot be equal.
